label: read-bm-contract
in_my_words: A team wants to offer a London design studio a small sample: a printed two-layer plastic strip that curls when the air gets damp, which could open or close a shade without a motor. Before building it, helpers read rules, safety sheets, grants and patents to see whether it could pass fire rules, who would pay, and who already owns similar ideas. The answer so far is that it probably can't be used on tall flats, nobody clearly pays for a design rule alone, and the offer should be measurements rather than promises.
how_in_my_words: Eight helpers each read a different pile of documents: building fire rules, printer-maker data, test standards, heat versus damp bending, safety sheets, grant lists, and patents. They saved pages and exact quotes. A second set of readers rechecked the main claims, and only confirmed ones are used. Unconfirmed ones are listed as left out. A short list of commands lets you redo some checks yourself.

test_questions.question: Why can't a printed plastic shade probably go on a tall block of flats in England?
test_questions.my_answer: For homes with a floor at 18 m or higher, outer wall parts must be nearly non-burning, and shading slats aren't exempt.

test_questions.question: Why can't a desk print be given a fire class?
test_questions.my_answer: A real fire class needs large test pieces.

test_questions.question: What would prove the team's bet wrong?
test_questions.my_answer: A firm paying for design rules alone, a printed resin earning the top fire class, or a measured energy saving from a damp-air shade.

test_questions.question: How much does the proof-of-concept sample cost to make?
Why leave two resins out of any public sample?
test_questions.my_answer: They carry a warning for harm to unborn children.

sentences_i_could_not_follow: We would also be wrong if a damp-air shade had a measured energy saving. The helpers searched and found none, but they could not search everywhere.
The claim that the bilayer ratio optimum appears in an older patent text citing Timoshenko: the page could not be fetched.
The claim that no patent pairs a theorem prover with material or print design: the checkers could not reach the search pages.
Our bet, written down before looking: nobody will pay for the rule alone, and no printed resin will pass the fire rules for tall homes.
The studio prints with robot arms and plant plastic, not with resin or powder, so our samples only prove the shape idea.
what_would_help: Open with a plain verdict (probably not for tall flats, nobody pays for rules alone) and say what the team actually offers the studio. Say who the team is, what the rule is, why a theorem prover is involved, and cut the jargon and unexplained acronyms.
